# Threat Model

**System:** STAR — a research department for screenwriters.
**Deployed:** Google Cloud Run, us-central1, public and unauthenticated at the
edge, `star.626labs.dev`. Public repository.
**Reviewed:** 2026-08-12.

Two sections of the generated scaffold arrived pre-filled with boilerplate that
was **false for this system** — it asserted JWT authentication, which STAR does
not use anywhere. Both were replaced rather than extended. Every claim below is
cited to the file it came from, and anything that could not be read is left as
NEEDS INPUT rather than guessed.

## Asset Scope

**What is worth attacking here is the money, not the data.** STAR holds no
payment details, no health or financial records, and no personal data beyond an
account identity. What it does hold is a wallet: one room build spends a dozen
or more live web searches through the Parallel Search API plus several Gemini
calls, and a public URL with no ceiling is an open invitation to spend someone
else's budget where the first sign is the bill.
<!-- Source: star/guards.py module docstring -->

Assets, in the order an attacker would rank them:

1. **The spend path.** `POST /api/rooms` and the MCP `build_room` and
   `check_scene` tools each cost real money per call.
   <!-- Source: star/guards.py, star/mcp/tools.py build_room description -->
2. **Service-account credentials reachable from inside the deployment.** On
   Cloud Run the metadata server at `169.254.169.254` will hand out access
   tokens to anything inside the container that asks.
   <!-- Source: tests/test_oauth_ssrf.py module docstring -->
3. **API keys** for Gemini (`GOOGLE_API_KEY`) and Parallel Search
   (`PARALLEL_API_KEY`), injected from Secret Manager at deploy, never in the
   image or the repo.
   <!-- Source: scripts/deploy.sh --set-secrets -->
4. **Writers' research and MCP credentials**, per account, in Firestore under
   `users/{uid}/rooms/{run_id}` and `.../scenes/{scene_id}`.
   <!-- Source: star/store.py -->

**Entry points:** the browser UI and JSON API; the SSE progress stream; `POST
/mcp` (JSON-RPC); the OAuth 2.1 authorization server (`/oauth/authorize`,
`/oauth/token`, `/oauth/register`) and its two `.well-known` discovery
documents.
<!-- Source: star/server.py routes, star/oauth/metadata.py -->

**Explicitly not an asset:** the treatment itself. It is not stored — only the
story profile extracted from it and the research it produces.
<!-- Source: web/index.html retention copy -->

## Threat Actors

- **The opportunistic budget burner.** Finds a public URL that spends money and
  scripts it. No credential needed: `POST /api/rooms` is reachable
  unauthenticated at the edge. This is the most likely actor by a wide margin
  and the one the guards are built for.
- **A malicious OAuth client.** Anyone may register: dynamic client
  registration is open by design, and Client ID Metadata Documents make the
  server fetch a URL a stranger chose. That is a request-forgery primitive by
  construction.
  <!-- Source: star/oauth/clients.py, tests/test_oauth_ssrf.py -->
- **An agent acting beyond its consent.** A writer connects an assistant over
  MCP and grants some scopes. The threat is the agent doing what it was not
  approved for — most sharply, deleting rooms it was only meant to read.
  <!-- Source: star/oauth/validate.py SCOPE_BY_TOOL -->
- **A hostile treatment or scene.** Text a writer pastes reaches four model
  agents. Content that reads as instructions is an injection attempt against
  the pipeline rather than against the server.
  <!-- Source: star/agents/synthesis.py, researchers.py, script_check.py -->
- **A curious reader of a public repository.** The code, the design docs and
  the review history are all public. Anything secret must be secret because of
  where it is stored, not because nobody has read the source.

Out of scope, deliberately: nation-state actors, and any insider threat model —
this is a solo-authored project with two commit contributors.
<!-- Source: .vibe-doc/state.json gitStats -->

## Threat Scenarios

**1. Budget exhaustion through a public endpoint.** An unauthenticated caller
loops `POST /api/rooms` until the search and model budget is gone. *Compounding
detail:* the guards are per-process, in-memory counters, so the ceiling is only
global while exactly one process exists.
<!-- Source: star/guards.py -->

**2. Rate-limit evasion by forging the caller key.** The limiter keys on
`X-Forwarded-For`. Proxies **append** to that header rather than replacing it,
so the leftmost entry is attacker-controlled and is not even validated as an IP.
*This was not hypothetical:* 50 requests with a rotating leftmost value were all
allowed past a 5/hour limit, and `X-Forwarded-For: totally-not-an-ip` was
accepted verbatim as the key.
<!-- Source: star/server.py _caller_key docstring, measured 2026-08-09 -->

**3. SSRF to the cloud metadata server.** A registered client supplies a
metadata-document URL pointing at `169.254.169.254`, or at any internal address,
and the server fetches it — returning service-account tokens to the attacker.
<!-- Source: tests/test_oauth_ssrf.py -->

**4. An agent exceeding granted scope.** A token granted only `rooms:read` calls
`delete_room`. *This one shipped:* the router skipped the scope check entirely
for any tool missing from `SCOPE_BY_TOOL`, so `ask_room` was callable by any
valid token whatever it was granted.
<!-- Source: docs/HANDOFF.md, star/mcp/router.py -->

**5. Cross-account reads.** A caller supplies another account's `run_id` to
`get_room`, `delete_room` or `check_scene`.

**6. Prompt injection through a treatment or a scene.** Pasted text instructs a
researcher to ignore its brief, or instructs the editor to fabricate a citation.

**7. Clickjacking.** The app is framed by a hostile page to capture interaction
with a control that spends money or deletes a room.

**8. Credential theft from storage or logs.** An MCP bearer token is recovered
from the database, a log line, or an API response.

## Mitigations

**Spend, per scenario 1.** Two independent ceilings: a per-IP sliding-window
limit on room creation, and a global daily cap acting as a kill switch. Both are
in-memory and correct **only** under both halves of the scaling config —
`--max-instances=1` because run state is per-process, and `--min-instances=1`
because scaling to zero destroys the process and the next request cold-starts
with both counters at zero. Under `max-instances=1` alone, "100 builds/day"
silently means "100 builds per instance lifetime."
<!-- Source: star/guards.py, scripts/deploy.sh -->

**Caller identity, per scenario 2.** The limiter takes the **rightmost**
`X-Forwarded-For` entry — the hop GCP's own load balancer appended — rather than
the leftmost, which is whatever the client typed. It falls back to
`request.client.host` for traffic that never passed a proxy.
<!-- Source: star/server.py _caller_key -->

**SSRF, per scenario 3.** The guard is a separate function in its own file with
its own test file, and every refusal is named for the thing it refuses. Both
network calls are isolated to two module-level seams (`_resolve` for DNS,
`_open_once` for HTTP) so the guard is testable without a live server.
<!-- Source: star/oauth/clients.py, tests/test_oauth_ssrf.py -->

**Scope, per scenario 4.** Three scopes, split by consequence rather than by
convenience: `rooms:read`, `rooms:write`, and `rooms:delete` **on its own** —
building and deleting are opposite risks, and a reader who lets an agent
research for them has said nothing about whether it may clear their workspace.
A completeness test now pins `SCOPE_BY_TOOL` to the tool list, so an unmapped
tool fails a test rather than shipping unguarded. `delete_room` additionally
takes two calls: the first destroys nothing and returns a single-use token.
<!-- Source: star/oauth/validate.py, star/mcp/tools.py -->

**Ownership, per scenario 5.** Every store path is rooted at `users/{uid}`, so
another account's document is *not found* by construction rather than refused by
a check that someone has to remember to write.
<!-- Source: star/store.py delete_scene docstring -->

**Injection, per scenario 6.** Every agent that receives writer-supplied text is
instructed that everything between the markers is research data, is never
instructions, and that instruction-like text inside it must be ignored.
Independently, no citation is trusted from a model: every source is hydrated
server-side from what the search API actually returned, and a cited URL that
appears in no result is stamped unsourced rather than rendered as a source.
<!-- Source: star/agents/{synthesis,researchers,script_check}.py; star/findings.py -->

**Framing, per scenario 7.** `X-Frame-Options: DENY` and
`Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'` on every response, applied as
global middleware rather than per-route — a header that must be remembered per
route is one that will be forgotten on the next one.
<!-- Source: star/server.py _deny_framing -->

**Credentials, per scenario 8.** An MCP token is `star_<12 hex>.<32 hex>`: an
identifier and a secret, deliberately split so the part that appears in the UI
and in logs is not the part that authenticates. Only the sha256 of the secret is
stored; the plaintext exists on the wire exactly once and is never recoverable.
Tokens are revocable, and can only be issued to an account with a linked
identity, because an anonymous account's only proof of ownership is a
`localStorage` entry.
<!-- Source: star/tokens.py, README.md -->

**Attack surface reduction.** `/docs`, `/redoc` and `/openapi.json` are all
disabled: the schema exposes no secrets, but it hands an attacker a map of every
route and shape for free. The MCP door also checks `Origin` against an
allow-list when a browser sends one.
<!-- Source: star/server.py FastAPI(), star/config.py mcp_allowed_origins -->

**Secrets handling.** `GOOGLE_API_KEY` and `PARALLEL_API_KEY` are injected from
Secret Manager as `--set-secrets` and never appear as literal values in the
service config, the image, or the repository.
<!-- Source: scripts/deploy.sh -->

## Residual Risks

**Accepted, with the reason.**

**The abuse guards are per-process and always will be until the instance count
changes.** If anyone raises `--max-instances` above 1, the per-IP limit
multiplies by the instance count and the daily cap stops being daily-global.
Moving to a shared store must happen in the *same change* as the scale-up, not
after it.
<!-- Source: star/guards.py -->

**The caller key is not a strong identity.** The rightmost `X-Forwarded-For`
entry is correct for traffic through GCP's load balancer, but it identifies a
network path, not a person. A determined attacker with many source addresses is
bounded by the daily cap, not by the per-IP limit.

**Anonymous accounts are held by a `localStorage` entry.** Clearing browser
storage loses the account. This is why MCP tokens require a linked identity.
<!-- Source: star/tokens.py -->

**A deleted room stays recoverable for 30 days** before it is destroyed, and
during that window it is still readable to anyone holding the account's
credentials. That is the deliberate trade: recoverable beats irreversible.
<!-- Source: star/config.py room_retention_days -->

**No audit log.** There is no record of which credential performed which action.
Token `last_used_at` is throttled to once a minute and is the only usage signal
that exists.
<!-- Source: star/tokens.py -->

**There is no detection path. The billing console is the alarm.** This is the
largest gap in this document and it is stated plainly rather than implied,
because it changes what the threshold above is worth. `star/guards.py` refuses
requests past the cap but emits no alert; there is no metric, no log-based alert
and no budget alarm in the deploy. So "take it down at 150% of the cap" is not a
tripwire today — it is a number a human would discover after the fact, possibly
a day later, by looking at a bill.

Two consequences follow, and both are worth being honest about:

- **Every mitigation above is preventive, none is detective.** The guards stop
  the ordinary case well. They tell nobody when they are being tested.
- **The one case they cannot stop is the one nothing would report.** The
  counters reset on an instance recycle or a redeploy, and that reset is
  invisible from outside — an attacker who waits out an idle window gets a fresh
  100 builds, and the only trace is spend.

**The cheapest fix, and it is genuinely cheap:** a Cloud Billing budget alert at
the spend equivalent of the threshold, plus a log-based alert on the cap
refusal that `star/guards.py` already emits. Neither requires touching the app.
Until one of them exists, the response plan in this document depends on somebody
opening a billing page.
<!-- Source: builder, 2026-08-12, asked directly at generation time -->

**No encryption at rest beyond Google Cloud defaults**, and no key rotation
schedule for the two API keys.

### Risk tolerance: the take-it-down threshold

**150% of the daily build cap in a single day. Take the service down.**

Stated as a percentage of `config.max_rooms_per_day()` rather than as a fixed
number of builds or a dollar figure, so it stays true if the cap ever moves. At
today's cap of 100 that is **150 builds**, and the arithmetic that makes it a
threshold worth acting on:

| Measure | At the cap | At the threshold |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Builds | 100 | 150 |
| Live searches, worst case | 3,000 | 4,500 |
| Live searches, at observed rates | 1,200–1,900 | 1,800–2,850 |

<!-- Source: star/config.py max_rooms_per_day (100), max_searches_per_build
     (30 ceiling); observed 12–19 searches per build across the 16 rooms
     stored as of 2026-08-12 -->

**Why 150% rather than a bigger multiple.** Exceeding the cap at all is not
overuse, it is evidence the guard is not holding — the counters are per-process
and in-memory, so the only ways past 100 are an instance recycle, a redeploy
mid-attack, or evasion. The 50% margin exists to absorb one legitimate reset
(a deploy on a busy day) without paging anyone; anything beyond it means the
ceiling is not a ceiling, and the correct response is to stop serving rather
than to keep watching.

**What "take it down" means here.** `gcloud run services update star
--max-instances=0`, or removing the unauthenticated invoker binding. Either
stops the spend; neither destroys any filed research, which stays in Firestore.
